title: Life has once again found a way in Athanasia, an "immersive" dinosaur FPS that feels like comfort food for Dino Crisis and System Shock players alike
description: Good news, people who figure they are going to die of old age before they get another Dino Crisis! Good news also, people who can't get enough throwback immersive sims! Even as Capcom forge ahead with their Resident Evil remake ouroboros, plucky Momentum Games and horror publishers Black Lantern Collective are releasing Athanasia - a first-person homage to both Dino Crisis and System Shock, in which you play intrepid researcher Carmen Flores, who has been sent to one of gaming's many ominous abandoned scientific facilities in South America. One of these days, I'm going to turf up to a collapsing laboratory complex in a game and discover nothing but stationery, old rubber gloves, and unfiled expense claims. I imagine a lot of laboratories are abandoned not due to (for example) gene-modded dilophosaurus outbreaks, but because the funders got cold feet long before Project X reached the prototyping stage. But that day is not this day. Today, there are dinosaurs! Argh, my face and/or intestines! Here's a trailer. Read more

title: WoW: Forever Hall of Thanes Dungeon Guide – Quests, Map, Bosses, and Loot
description: Historically, the first time you’d step into a World of Warcraft dungeon as part of The Alliance is The Deadmines. However, World of Warcraft: Forever introduces a new low-level instance called The Hall of Thanes that dishes out blue quality gear like candy on Halloween, getting your character off to a flying start. It’s effectively the Alliance version of Ragefire Chasm, making it the perfect spot to dust off your mechanical cobwebs if it’s been a hot minute, or learn fundamentals if you’re a beginner dungeoneer. Here, we’ll take you through everything you need to know about WoW: Forever's Hall of Thanes. This includes how to get there, how to clear all five of its associated quests, boss strategies, and, of course, a full rundown of all the juicy loot you can acquire. Based on its difficulty, we’d recommend abstaining from HoT until you reach level 14. The extra spells from this milestone are likely to come in handy, regardless of your class. How to get to Hall of Thanes Hall of Thanes is located in Old Ironforge, which is accessible from The High Seat in Ironforge. Getting to Hall of Thanes could not be easier if you rolled a dwarf or gnome, as you’ll naturally start your journey in Dun Morogh. If you find yourself in Stormwind first, simply take the Deeprun Tram from the Dwarven District to Ironforge. If you’re a Night Elf hailing from Darnassus, you luckily won’t have to make janky death runs from Menethil Harbor or brave the Wetlands like the old days. First thing’s first, take the portal to Rut’theran Village, before hopping on a boat to Auberdine in Darkshore. From there, board the new ship that takes you directly to Stormwind. Step onto the tram, and you’re good to go. Now in Ironforge, make your way to The High Seat, which is accessible from The Great Forge (around 44, 52). As soon as you’re inside, hook a left, follow the stairs down, and you’ll end up in Old Ironforge. Hall of Thanes Map Map created by Santiago Reyes (2026) The route through Hall of…

title: Xbox Game Pass Is Losing 8 More Games In October
description: It's that time of month when Xbox updates the Game Pass library, and, as usual, a few more games are leaving the subscription service in a few weeks. On October 31, you can say goodbye to 8 more games, including a few LucasArts classics, a diggy-diggy blast of co-op fun, and one of the biggest Lego Star Wars games of all time. With Double Fine no longer part of the Xbox Game Studios family, it looks like two of the studio's best remasters will be leaving soon. The remastered editions of Full Throttle and Day of the Tentacle are on their way out, so if you haven't checked out these classic '90s point-and-click adventures, now is a great time to do so. Each one features high-resolution artwork and remastered audio. You'll also want to grab the action-packed co-op shooter Deep Rock Galactic, the strategic RPG Wartales, and the PvPvE multiplayer shooter Wildgate, which fuses ship-to-ship combat with fast-paced action. Dead Static Drive is a hidden gem best described as Grand Theft Cthulhu, while Lara Croft and the Temple of Osiris is a top-notch co-op game that lets even more players join the intrepid archaeologist on her expeditions. Finally, Lego Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga is a massive game that covers all nine movies in the classic sci-fi series, and like a bucket of Lego, it can keep you entertained for hours. Leaving Xbox Game Pass on October 31 Full Throttle Remastered Dead Static Drive Wildgate Deep Rock Galactic Day of the Tentacle Remastered Wartales Full Throttle Remastered Lego Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga Lara Croft and the Temple of Osiris As a reminder, you can save 20% on these games if you decide to buy them before they leave Game Pass. At the start of the month, nine games left Xbox Game Pass, with the critically acclaimed Expedition 33: Clair Obscur as the biggest departure. Other notable exits included The Casting of Frank Stone, A Plague Tale: Requiem, Donut County, and Evil West.

title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Relics Guide
description: The Castlevania series is no stranger to introducing game-breaking relics. Who could forget the Duplicator from Symphony of the Night, which let you reuse Library Cards to warp to the librarian's shop, throw infinite Buffalo Stars to destroy the toughest bosses, and chug endless healing potions, as long as it was equipped? In the same game, the Ring of Varda's stat buffs alone made every fight trivial. Other Castlevania adventures also had their fair share of items that exploited that game's individual mechanics, so a dedicated Relics menu opens up plenty of possibilities. With over 40 options available, perhaps we'll see a combination of stuff that breaks this metroidvania wide open. In any case, you can only equip three at a time, so here are the best Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Relic combos and all of their locations. The Relics menu has plenty of options to choose from, but only three slots. Choose wisely! How many relics are there in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse? There are 44 individual relics in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse. You can equip up to three at once, each granting a tangible perk to Rose's combat abilities and spells. Rose is stuck between two sets of Bone Pillars spitting fireballs, just as an Axe Knight springs to life. The best Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Relic combos Stacking damage-dealing relics to trigger after certain conditions are met is key to maximizing efficiency. However, we recommend you have a trio of other relics in mind to swap to whenever taking on boss fights. For regular traversal, the combination of Obsidian Fang and Necro Charm can help massively with larger groups of foes. For example, if you go up against one of the lance knights and parry their attacks, they will become stunned, making for an easy kill. After killing them, you can do more damage to a nearby cluster of enemies. Bosses require you to study their patterns to determine the relics best suited for the job. If you find yourself stabbing them in the back, the Vile…

title: How to descend the Catacombs of Paris in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse
description: After gathering all three keys by defeating Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse 's first three bosses--The Fallen, Joan of Arc, and Medusa--you should then return to the room where Rose fought the first of the bunch. Here, she will place three stones into the door and descend into the Catacombs. This marks the first really difficult area to navigate as it’s long and winding, with plenty of traps and enemies blocking your spelunking efforts. To conquer this area, you’ll need to get to grips with using Holy Light to phase in and out of Chaos Shards, dodge deadly spinning discs, and fight against some of the toughest regular enemies you’ve seen so far in this metroidvania adventure. The worst bit is that it’s not the only majorly tricky, prolonged area you need to navigate; the Clock Tower is definitely more complex and deadly. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves. Here is how to descend the Catacombs in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse. Rose encounters some Bone Pillars during a precarious drop near some spinning blades. How to descend the Catacombs As you enter, head down and to the left to the next room. This next room will have some ghosts, bone pillars, and exploding spiders in addition to the regular skeleton archers and other nasties you’ve faced so far. Use Holy Light to cross the Chaos Shard blocks and reach the next room. This one introduces Fleamen, who hop around and can latch onto you if they hit. Parrying will be effective against most enemies here, so take your time. After some more enemies, you’ll need to go down a shaft filled with spinning blades. Time your jumps well and use the grapples you find later on, and you should reach the bottom and the next room. Believe it or not, that was the easy part! But first, follow the glowing trail to the left to find a save room. Head left and cross the skull head. Keep going left and you’ll see a ledge above you can take to grab one of the Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse relics, or continue to the green writing on the wall.…

title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Alucard Painting Puzzle Explained
description: For a fan-favorite character, the lack of Alucard in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse may be somewhat surprising. However, those who actually read the intro to Symphony of the Night will know that after the events that led to Lord of Darkness's first demise at the hands of a Belmont, the dhampir went into what he thought was an eternal slumber to rid the world of his accursed bloodline. However, he's still in the latest metroidvania adventure... sort of. You see, someone has decorated the main hall with a bunch of Alucard's portraits. One of Dracula's talking statues hints that these paintings have a hidden meaning. So we'll go over exactly what they mean and why you need to seek them out. This statue gives us a not-so-subtle hint as to what the deal is with all these Alucard paintings. Alucard's Paintings hidden meaning In the Main Hall area of the castle, you'll encounter paintings of Alucard, Dracula's son. They're so important that they even show up on the area map. However, it's not initially clear why there are so many of them. According to a statue in the Servant's Hall, part of the Main Hall, "The Artiste chose to honor one who left your side too soon. The Master's son will point the way, his face still makes us swoon." The key line is about pointing the way, and that's exactly what Alucard is doing with his sword. Each painting hints at a secret passage: whether it's the hidden entrance to the Artist's studio, a hidden weapon or one of the many relics, the entrance to the Waterworks area, or even the path leading to one of the more complex sidequests in the game. So if the painting is pointing downward, treat it as if the floor is passable and drop through. If the sword faces upward or to the side, you can enter one of the blank paintings with the Arcane Whip and launch Rose in that direction to reveal a hidden path. Once you know the secret, reading that painting's meaning is as simple as following directions!

title: How To Climb The Clock Tower In Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse
description: Having made your way into Dracula's Castle, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse throws a rather huge curveball almost immediately: a long ascent up the Clock Tower. Now, veterans of the metroidvania series will know making it to the top is no easy feat, with these areas typically housing some fiendish spike traps, flying enemies, and large drops. The Clock Tower in Belmont's Curse is the most devilish yet, with spinning blades ready to slice you up if you so much as brush past them. On top of that, you've been challenged by the Zealot, a previous boss who says he'll only fight you at the summit. Naturally, you want all of Dracula's minions dead, so here's how to reach the Clock Tower's peak. Occasionally, you'll need to use enemies as stepping stones to reach the top. How to reach the top of the Clock Tower From the get-go, there are perils to heading up the Clock Tower. The first room has giant iron fists that pound the ground whenever you get close. They won't kill you, but they do hurt a lot. The first vertical room has some Medusa Heads you can latch onto to get some height, but be careful of the spinning blades in the middle of the giant wheels. You'll also need to duck under the spikes at the top to avoid being sent back to the bottom. The next room introduces two new things: the iron fists can push switches to rotate platforms (more on that later), and there are many Nova Skeletons blasting full-screen lasers out of their bellies in the latest Castlevania game. The next vertical shaft requires you to leap across the rotating platforms at the top while avoiding the laser beams, but is otherwise unremarkable. When you reach the top of the next room, there is a faint glow leading to the left. Follow it to find a save room and a shortcut back to the bottom. From this point, you can go east until you reach the Library, but you also have plenty of Clock Tower to climb. Notable obstacles include the wheels of spinning saws in the Eastern Steps that slowly roll down…

title: All Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse Weapon Locations
description: Castlevania games typically have relatively simple combat. You press a button and a whip, sword, or other weapon usually comes out swinging. It's not usually complex with combos outside of the Lords of Shadow era, with the series typically focused more on exploration than a thrilling set of moves. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse significantly changes these combat mechanics as Rose has access to seven weapon families, complete with buffs and perks. Each type has four different possible upgrades you can find on your journey, with subsequent weapons recovered from grand chests. To find the best weapons in this metroidvania, you'll occasionally need to think outside the box and find hidden rooms in seemingly unassuming passages. Each weapon type in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has four slots, with those further right being more powerful. All Castlevania: Belmont's Curse weapons While you start with the humble Longsword, rather than the Vampire Killer whip a Belmont would typically wield to smite Dracula's monstrous army, Rose is proficient with seven different types. Here are all the weapons in the game and their locations: Sword The sword is a quick weapon type that will do more damage to enemies if they're hit immediately after a backdash or slide. You can also use the Arcane Whip on enemies with the sword equipped to dash through them when it connects. Longsword: Paris Streets - Bank of the River Seine (Unlocked at the beginning of the game.) Bastard Sword: Paris Streets - Justice District Sewers (From the area that leads east toward the Main Castle gate, instead turn back left and head toward the Ferryman warp. In this room, you'll need to time your rope swinging to avoid blades and go through Chaos Shards. Lower the bridge to the left and back up the Chaos Shard column to reach the top of the room and the chest.) Joyeuse: Currently unknown Valmanway: Currently unknown Shortsword & Shield These two weapons bridge attack and defense, with regular presses hitting…

title: How To Solve The Hidden Puzzle In Notre Dame In Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse
description: Getting into Notre Dame in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has its challenges. However, the Cathedral itself is home to a giant organ that the Shadow Arcana boss has used to seal himself away from you. Of course, this is Death, and he doesn't make it easy, but finding the ghosts in Notre Dame will give you the three melodies you need to play to unlock the door and fight him. But what if we told you that, despite beating Death, there is actually a fourth melody you can play? The Shadow Arcana spells hint at another tune, but this time there's no ghost to tell you which keys to press. You'll need to venture into one specific room that's thankfully close to a save room, so we'll explain where to go and how to figure out which keys to press to finish this metroidvania 's most fiendish puzzle yet. Paying attention to background details will reveal a bunch of hidden information. How to find and decipher the hidden melody The first step to completing this puzzle is to visit the Stained Glass Gallery in Notre Dame. From the Western Triforium save point, head right, jumping down the hole at the top, past the Ferryman room, and into the Sealed Scriptorium. From there, go right and crash through the Stained Glass Gallery's ceiling. Notice the symbols at the top of the windows? These are in the same order as the keys on the Giant Organ, while the candles below them are the sequence for playing the hidden melody. In total, the tune consists of ten key presses, and you'll definitely need the double jump and dash power-ups to play them. Now that you know the tune, you can play it to unlock a bunch of stuff at the same time! How to play the Notre Dame hidden melody Go to the Giant Organ and make your way to the Crescent Moon key. From here, you'll need to play the following keys: Moon Libra (Right one key) Scorpio (Right one key) Aquarius (Right three keys) Capricorn (Left one key) Virgo (Left six keys) Sun (Right one key) Leo (Left two keys) Cancer (Left one key) Aries (Left three…

title: How To Enter Notre Dame in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse
description: Chances are, if you're reading this, you are a little stuck as to how to proceed in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse after falling for Death's trap. After all, that pesky clock is part of the problem, warping Rose to Dracula's lair before she's meant to fight him and leading to a less-than-desirable outcome. So if you don't want the worst Castlevania: Belmont's Curse ending, you'll need to find a lead. Naturally, with a castle so labyrinthine in its design, there are potential leads everywhere you look. However, one early example you may have seen is a giant painting of Notre Dame Cathedral, just hanging there in a giant hallway. Those who have played Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin might have an inkling of what this means, but you'll need to gather a few key items together before you can explore this hidden area. When you eventually find all the components, return to this painting to bring it to life. Where is Notre Dame in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse? Surprisingly, finding Notre Dame is remarkably simple. In the Main Hall, as you progress toward the Clock Tower area, you'll come across a large empty hallway with a giant painting of the famous French cathedral. You won't be able to do anything with this artwork right now, but it's essential that you do visit at some point if you want to finish the game. With the power gained from Talos, you can destroy this grotesque marble statue. Requirements for unlocking Notre Dame Your first objective is to find and defeat Talos. He is an extremely well-hidden boss that requires a bit of puzzle-solving to reach his lair, and the fight is relatively tricky too. You can find more detail on how to get to the Talos boss fight toward the end of our How to Ascend the Clock Tower guide, as this is the true main boss of the area. Once you have beaten Talos, you'll obtain his technique that breaks specific barriers and objects with a yellow glow. This is needed for the next step: unlocking the Artist Arcana. In the Main Hall area, you'll…

title: Win 19 Castlevania Games And Two DLCs In This Fangtastic Giveaway
description: As someone who has been enjoying the monster-infested streets of Paris (said in a French accent), Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse has made me fall in love with the decades-old series once again. Of course, many of these games were released before I was even born, and chances are, that’s the case for you, too--but don’t worry! You can catch up with this excellent giveaway for a chance to win 19 Castlevania games, two DLCs for the brilliant Lords of Shadow, and a book to boot. Try fitting that in a coffin. While Belmont’s Curse is the most recent entry, the Castlevania series is full of bangers. The original games are retro goodness, seeing you deal with an onslaught of monsters in frustratingly fun ways. Sure, they have some annoying elements--looking near you, Medusa Heads. Not at you; you can’t fool me. But that’s part of the charm, and the earliest entries are a great way to see how far the series has come. Personally, I’m a big fan of Super Castlevania IV. That whip swing? Timeless. Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow and Dawn of Sorrow are excellent, too, with the former being one of the best in the entire series. Aria of Sorrow is well-paced (goodbye, tedious backtracking), with a big arsenal of weapons that all feel unique and fun to use. As an added bonus, completing the game unlocks a new mode that will bring a smile to anyone’s face after playing the older experiences. Lords of Shadow and Lords of Shadow 2 were actually my first Castlevania titles, despite being remarkably different from the earlier games. They’re still great, though. While the latter suffers from FSSS (Forced Stealth Section Syndrome), its hack-and-slash gameplay, in a similar vein to God of War and Devil May Cry, will have character-action fans like myself having a great time. And while Mirror of Fate adopts a 2.5D perspective, it feels like a great balance between old and modern, bridging the gap between the classic Castlevania games and the hack-and-slash gameplay of the Lords of Shadow…

title: Fire Emblem’s Remarkable Comeback
description: Though it may not be a sales juggernaut on the scale of Mario or The Legend of Zelda, Fire Emblem is one of Nintendo's preeminent franchises. Like so many of its vaunted stablemates, the series is almost as old as Nintendo's gaming ambitions, debuting on the Famicom and appearing on nearly every home and handheld console since. Given this prominence, it's almost difficult to believe that Fire Emblem's future was ever in jeopardy, but such was indeed once the case; there was a point in time when the series was very much on the verge of cancellation, and it took a dramatic shakeup to reverse its fortunes. To fully contextualize this rocky period in Fire Emblem's history, we need to look back at its trajectory in the wake of its belated international debut. Unlike Nintendo's other marquee properties, Fire Emblem took a circuitous route to Western markets. Though the series began in 1990, its first several installments were never released outside of Japan, and most Western players would end up being introduced to the franchise not through one of its mainline entries, but through Super Smash Bros. Melee for the Nintendo GameCube. Even more so than its predecessor, Melee was a veritable celebration of Nintendo history. The game drew deeply from the company's rich oeuvre; its roster was stuffed with beloved mascots, and its extensive array of collectible trophies covered the full sweep of the publisher's gaming legacy, from renowned classics to obscure curios. What generated the most chatter among international players, however, were two particular hidden fighters who hailed from a series most had never heard of: Marth, hero of the first Fire Emblem, and Roy, protagonist of the series' then-newest installment, The Binding Blade. Despite their unfamiliarity, these mysterious swordsmen instantly became two of Melee's most popular characters thanks to their cool designs and nimble swordplay, which helped set them apart from the more recognizable characters on the roster.…

title: Tenebris Somnia Blends 2D Visuals With Live-Action Horror Scenes, And It’s Already On Sale At Launch
description: Horror games live or die by their scares and tension. If the player isn’t uncomfortable guiding a character through dreadful situations, well, you may as well be playing an action-adventure game (don’t mention the first Uncharted’s final act, please). Tenebris Somnia blends the discomfort of retro horror with live-action sequences that will make your goosebumps bump, and you can get it cheaper than ever right now. As the best horror games continue to push for more realistic visuals and immersive experiences, Tenebris Somnia’s twist on the genre combines old-school cool with movie-like cutscenes. It’s both jarring and original, and that’s exactly what makes for excellent horror. I want to be constantly surprised, and Tenebris Somnia makes its pixelated 2D threats even more menacing when you see live-action versions of the monsters. Inspired by classics that scared us silly, like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, Tenebris Somnia has a deceptively simple premise. You play as Julia, who finds herself in a parallel universe while visiting her ex-boyfriend and is relentlessly hunted by nightmares that, well, aren’t exactly figments of her imagination. (To be honest, visiting an ex sounds like a nightmarish experience on its own. Ba-dum, tsss.) Co-created by Andrés Borghi and Tobías Rusjan with Saibot Studios, and published by New Blood Interactive, the studio behind Ultrakill, Blood West, and Gloomwood, Tenebris Somnia’s style is fittingly inspired by past eras of console gaming. Its pixelated visuals make the switch to live-action cutscenes even more unsettling. It’s almost like Clock Tower, but if it randomly turned into a movie at any second. No, I’m not shaking; you are. If you’re looking to rewind to those retro vibes while adding something new to your scary movie marathon this spooky season, you can grab a Steam key for Tenebris Somnia for just $18.24 / £13.13 at Fanatical. That makes it a tempting way to experience a brand-new and genuinely unusual horror game for…

title: The Sunday Papers
description: Sundays are for firing up Twine again and thinking you know what, if this swanky IF plotter had been around when I was an undergraduate, I might have preserved all my exam revision notes in text adventure form. I still have two, reassuringly heavy boxes of tabbed and colour-coded index cards that you could plausibly lay out to form a maze, navigable by compass commands. Head down the western corridor from Middle English to the Renaissance, and – ah, bollocks, you have been eaten by a Grue. Surely somebody's thought of this, in the decade and change since Twine was released? I mean, we already have 3D museum exhibits extracted from Wikipedia. Sundays are also for heading to the allotment and getting annoyed with the tomato plants, who have decided to go bonkers right at the end of the growing season. I thought you were done, pesky nightshades. I thought I could leave you alone for the rest of the year. Finally, Sundays are for sharing good criticism, like the below. Read more

title: Rain98 is a blue-hued, pre-Y2K, Serial Experiments Lain inspired visual novel about time travelling to the past to end the world
description: Picture this. You're me, and you boot up the demo for Rain98, an incredibly blue-looking, rainy visual novel set in Tokyo, 1998, about a woman who refers to herself as the Angolmois, a world-ending reference to the predictions of good ole Nostradamus. At one point you have to light this woman's cigarette in a lightly stylish sequence. You get to a bit where you're asked to put your name in, and you put it in because like its predecessors, this is surely a self-insert kind of situation. Only you get a Steam achievement for getting a game over for putting your name in. Rude! But curious, so you, and of course I mean I, pressed on. Read more
